claims.text: A data-driven surrogate model can predict conductivity of HfNbTaTiZr across 0–200 K and 300–1200 K more accurately than conventional analytical models.
The target material is bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
Standard processing of this material produces realistic defects and grain-size distributions.
The surrogate will be trained on conductivity measurements from 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Grain size, defect density, and oxygen content will be explicit model inputs.
The model is intended to apply to bulk HfNbTaTiZr specimens containing about 1 wt.% oxygen.
Conductivity data from 200–300 K will be withheld as a blind test set.
Grain size and defect density mediate the influence of interstitial oxygen and defects on conductivity.
Interstitial oxygen and defects scatter electronic or phononic carriers and thereby alter conduction pathways.
Directly modeling defect- and oxygen-induced scattering overcomes limitations of defect-free analytical predictions.
The machine-learning model will learn empirical relationships among microstructure, composition, temperature, and conduction.
Learning these empirical relationships will improve prediction accuracy.
The surrogate will predict electrical or thermal conductivity in the held-out 200–300 K interval within a 15% error margin.
The surrogate will outperform conventional analytical models that omit microstructural imperfections.
Conventional analytical conductivity predictions assume perfect crystals and neglect defect and oxygen scattering.
Such conventional analytical predictions typically have larger errors for real defect-bearing materials.
Accuracy outside the stated temperatures, oxygen level, and microstructural domain is untested.
The quantitative improvement depends on the quality and coverage of the training data and microstructural characterization.
The benchmark will compare predictions from a model trained outside 200–300 K against independently measured conductivity within that interval.
An absolute percentage error exceeding 15% in the 200–300 K interval will falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The boundary restricts validity to 0–200 K and 300–1200 K, while the predicted outcome and decisive benchmark require predictions in the excluded 200–300 K interval.
